analysis.one_liner: Charges fossil fuel companies for carbon emissions and returns the money through tax credits, benefit checks, and a corporate tax cut.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2015, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge companies $45 for every ton of carbon dioxide released by burning coal, oil, and natural gas, with the charge rising each year, and would add fees on methane leaks and other greenhouse gases. It would return that money in several ways: up to $500 per worker per year as a refundable tax credit, $500 per year to Social Security, veterans', and disability beneficiaries, and $20 billion in annual grants to states to help low-income and rural households with energy bills and to retrain fossil fuel workers. It would also cut the corporate tax rate from 35 percent to 29 percent and protect American manufacturers by refunding fees on exports and charging equivalent fees on carbon-intensive imports.
analysis.who_benefits: Working people would get up to $500 a year (6.2 percent of earnings, whichever is smaller) through a refundable tax credit, even if they owe no income tax. Social Security, veterans', and disability beneficiaries would each get $500 a year. Low-income and rural households would get help with energy bills through state-run rebate programs, and displaced fossil fuel workers would get retraining and transition help. Everyone would benefit from lower carbon emissions, since the fee rises automatically until emissions fall to 20 percent of 2005 levels. Corporations and their shareholders would also gain from the 6-point cut in the corporate tax rate.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, retirees, disabled veterans, and low-income households

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a fee starting at $45 per ton of carbon dioxide on coal, petroleum products, and natural gas, rising 2 percent a year plus inflation, until U.S. emissions fall below 20 percent of 2005 levels [S3].
Provides a fully refundable tax credit of up to $500 per year ($1,000 for joint filers) to workers, and $500 annual payments to Social Security, veterans', and disability beneficiaries [S2][S3].

Directs $20 billion a year (adjusted for inflation) in grants to states to rebate energy costs to households below 150 percent of the poverty line, help rural households, and provide job training and transition assistance to fossil fuel workers [S3].
Protects manufacturers from losing ground to foreign competitors by refunding fees on exported energy-intensive goods and charging an equivalent fee on carbon-intensive imports [S3].
Requires a public website disclosing how much revenue the fee raises and where the benefits go [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel companies and, through passed-through prices, consumers of gasoline, heating fuel, and coal- and gas-fired electricity. Energy users who burn a lot of fuel — long-distance drivers, homes heated with oil or propane — could pay more in fees than they get back in credits. The bill offsets much of that burden with credits and grants, but it also redirects a large share of the revenue to a corporate tax cut, meaning shareholders capture money that could otherwise have gone to larger household rebates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and heavy energy consumers

drawbacks.text: The carbon fee would raise prices for gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity, and households with above-average energy use could pay more in fees than they receive in credits, especially before state grants ramp up [S3].

Cutting the corporate rate from 35 percent to 29 percent channels a substantial share of the carbon fee revenue to corporations and shareholders rather than to households, which was a deliberate trade to attract business support [S3].

The fee rises automatically every year by law, so Congress would have to act to slow it if energy prices spiked, and the program depends heavily on Treasury regulations for methane fees and border adjustments [S3].

Workers who do not file tax returns or who lack stable addresses could miss the credit, and state participation in the rebate program is optional, so help for low-income households could vary by state [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is genuinely progressive in its household provisions: the fee falls hardest on fossil fuel producers and the biggest energy users, while most working and retired households get roughly their money back through credits and payments. The main honest objections are the price shock for energy-heavy households and businesses, the large slice of revenue handed to a corporate rate cut, and heavy reliance on Treasury to get the methane and border-adjustment rules right. On the merits it is a serious, detailed attempt at a carbon tax with visible revenue return, not a narrow industry handout — but it never got a hearing, so none of these tradeoffs were tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in June 2015 and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill, with Sen. Brian Schatz as its only cosponsor, on June 10, 2015 [S1][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
The action history shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers avoided a $45-per-ton carbon fee, and corporations kept the 35 percent corporate tax rate rather than seeing it cut alongside new fees. Ordinary households received neither the carbon fee's burden nor its credits and grants, and emissions stayed on their pre-existing path.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers and untaxed carbon emissions

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsor and cosponsor were Democrats; with no votes ever taken there is no roll-call record, but the bill died in committee under Republican control of the Senate and the Finance Committee.

industries.note: The bill puts a $45-per-ton fee on coal and adds a supplementary fee covering methane from coal mining, falling hardest on this most carbon-intensive fuel [S3]. The fee is the point: it is designed to push electricity generation away from coal, which is where the public benefit lies [S3].

Fees apply at the refinery, terminal, and processor level on petroleum products and natural gas, and rise over time [S3]. The costs would be passed to consumers at the pump and on heating and utility bills, partially offset for households by the credits and state grants [S3].

The bill cuts the top corporate tax rate from 35 percent to 29 percent [S3]. This redirects a large share of the carbon fee revenue to corporate profits rather than to larger household benefits, which is why the bill's direction is genuinely mixed.

The bill imposes fees on fluorinated greenhouse gases produced or imported in the United States [S3]. These are potent warming gases, so the fee targets an industrial niche whose emissions carry outsize climate cost.

Border adjustments refund the carbon fee cost of exported manufactured goods and charge equivalent fees on carbon-intensive imports, shielding American factories from cheaper dirtier competition [S3]. This protects manufacturing jobs alongside the climate goal.
Companies that capture and securely store carbon dioxide from their emissions get a full refund of the fee, creating a direct financial reward for capture technology [S3].
